title: Expertise in pictorial perception: eye-movement patterns and visual memory in artists and laymen
research_question: How do eye-movement patterns and visual memory differ between artists and artistically untrained participants when viewing various types of pictures (from ordinary scenes to abstraction) under free scanning and memory instructions?

participants.description: 9 artists (25-50 years old, 5-11 years of art education, trained with models) and 9 artistically untrained participants (22-37 years old, graduate program/staff at Dept of Psychology). All had normal/corrected-to-normal vision and no color blindness. Both groups had undergone rigorous selection procedures in their respective fields.
participants.recruitment: Artists recruited from National College of Arts and Crafts and National Academy of Fine Art, Oslo. Untrained participants from Department of Psychology, University of Oslo.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 16 photographs edited in Adobe Photoshop, categorized into four groups: 'mundane' (uncomposed, ordinary scenes with human features and recognizable objects), 'good' (aesthetically pleasing, human features, recognizable objects), 'edited' (human features with more or less abstract, uniform surroundings), and 'abstract' (no human features or recognizable objects). Regions of Interest (ROIs) were subjectively defined on identifiable human or object features.

measures.construct: Percentage of viewing time within Regions of Interest (ROIs)

measures.instrument: Verbal recall test (mini-disc recorder, scored by categories)

measures.construct: Number of correctly remembered pictorial features (conceptual, configurational, form/colour)

mechanisms: Artistic training leads to an increased preference for viewing more abstract, structural features over familiar objects in pictures.
Artists' eye-movement patterns are modulated by task demands (e.g., memory task) and viewing time, unlike untrained participants.
Artists' viewing becomes more object-oriented when attempting to remember pictures.
The absence of repetition effects (fewer and longer fixations in second viewing) in artists may indicate a deviation from normal viewing strategies, potentially affecting encoding variability.
Artists are more skilled at extracting and remembering a greater variety of visual features due to its relevance in picture production.
Artists' scanning behavior is linked to training in figurative rendition, which requires apprehending exact physical features over general conceptual associations.
Figurative rendition training enhances attention to exact physical properties, which is a form of training effect.
Artists' superior memory for pictorial details is not attributable to guessing.

Artists' processing of spatial relations emphasizes coordinate visual properties (precise locations, metric units) over categorical representations (general properties), which is crucial for drawing/painting real models.
Preconceptions of what a model 'is' can interfere with the ability to accurately perceive it (as noted by Gombrich and Edwards).
Laymen's portrait drawing patterns may mirror their typical eye-scanning patterns (Yarbus).

limitations: The nature of the abstract pictures themselves (e.g., presence of striking focal areas, brightness, and color contrasts) can strongly influence global/local saccade ratios, potentially explaining less dramatic differences found compared to previous studies.

The unexpected finding that artists do not demonstrate repetition effects (fewer and longer fixations in a second viewing) is difficult to fully account for and may indicate a radical deviation from normal viewing strategies.

paper_metadata.title: Expertise in Pictorial Perception: Eye-Movement Patterns and Visual Memory in Artists and Laymen
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Expertise in Pictorial Perception: Eye-Movement Patterns and Visual Memory in Artists and Laymen
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: In two sessions with free scanning and memory instructions, eye-movement patterns from nine artists were compared with those of nine artistically untrained participants viewing 16 pictures representing a selection of categories from ordinary scenes to abstraction: 12 pictures were made to accommodate an object-oriented viewing mode (selection of recognisable objects), and a pictorial viewing mode (selection of more structural features), and 4 were abstract. The artistically untrained participants showed preference for viewing human features and objects, while the artists spent more scanning time on structural/abstract features. A group by session interaction showed a change of viewing strategy in the artists, who viewed more objects and human features in the memory task session. A verbal test of recall memory showed no overall difference in the number of pictures remembered, but the number of correctly remembered pictorial features was significantly higher for artists than for the artistically untrained viewers, irrespective of picture type. No differences in fixation frequencies/durations were found between groups across sessions, but a significant task-dependent-group by session interaction of fixation frequency/duration showed that the artistically untrained participants demonstrated repetition effects in fewer, longer fixations with repeated viewing, while the opposite pattern obtained for the artists.
